title: Dinosaurs: How They Lived, How They Died, and How We Know
department: Department of Earth Sciences, Paleontology Program
description: An introduction to dinosaurs for readers with no background in geology or biology. The course explains what makes an animal a dinosaur, how fossils form and how rocks are dated, the main dinosaur groups, and what bones, eggs, footprints and fossil feathers reveal about how dinosaurs grew, moved and behaved. It follows one line of small feathered dinosaurs into the birds alive today and examines the asteroid impact that ended the age of the non-avian dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Throughout, every claim is tied to the evidence and methods paleontologists use, and settled findings are kept apart from open questions.
objectives: Define a dinosaur by its anatomy and family tree, and distinguish dinosaurs from pterosaurs, marine reptiles and other prehistoric animals.
Explain how fossils form and how rocks are dated, and place the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous on the geologic time scale.
Name the major dinosaur groups and identify a skeleton's group from its key features.
Explain how bone microstructure, eggs, trackways and fossil feathers reveal growth, metabolism and behavior.
Explain the evidence that birds are living dinosaurs.
Evaluate the evidence for the asteroid impact and for volcanism in the end-Cretaceous extinction.
Use the Paleobiology Database to find where, and in what rocks, a dinosaur has been found.

sections.title: Reading rock layers

sections.title: Ornithischians

chapters.title: Growing Up Dinosaur
chapters.summary: How growth rings in bone and fossil eggs, nests and babies reveal how fast dinosaurs grew and how they cared for their young.

sections.title: Reading growth rings in bone
sections.summary: Thin sections of bone and the yearly lines of arrested growth, read like tree rings.

sections.title: Growth curves and growth spurts
sections.summary: How Tyrannosaurus grew fastest in its teenage years, and what growth rates suggest.

sections.title: Eggs and nests
sections.summary: Egg shapes and clutches, and the evidence that some early dinosaurs laid soft-shelled eggs.

sections.title: Parenting

chapters.title: Warm Blood, Feathers and Color
chapters.summary: The evidence on dinosaur metabolism, the feathered dinosaurs of China and elsewhere, and how fossil pigment structures reveal color.

sections.title: Warm-blooded, cold-blooded or in between

sections.title: Feathered dinosaurs
sections.summary: Sinosauropteryx and the feathered fossils of the Jehol Biota, and the range of feather types.

sections.title: Dinosaur colors

sections.title: Changing pictures of dinosaurs
sections.summary: From sluggish lizards to active animals, and how paleoartists work from evidence.

chapters.title: How Dinosaurs Lived
chapters.summary: What trackways, teeth, stomach contents, injuries and bonebeds reveal about how dinosaurs moved, fed and lived together.
chapters.challenge: Estimate a dinosaur's speed from a trackway using footprint length and stride length, stating every assumption.

sections.title: Footprints and speed
sections.summary: Trackways, stride length and Alexander's formula for estimating speed.

sections.title: What dinosaurs ate
sections.summary: Teeth, jaws, fossil dung and stomach contents.

sections.title: Herds, packs and bonebeds

sections.title: Spinosaurus and the water question

chapters.title: Birds: The Dinosaurs That Survived
chapters.summary: The evidence that birds evolved from small feathered theropods, from Archaeopteryx to the toothed birds of the Cretaceous, and how flight began.
chapters.challenge: List ten features shared by Velociraptor and a chicken, and say which ones appeared first in non-avian dinosaurs.

sections.title: Archaeopteryx
sections.summary: The 19th-century fossil with feathers, teeth and a bony tail, and where it sits among feathered dinosaurs.

sections.title: Ostrom and the dinosaur renaissance
sections.summary: John Ostrom's study of Deinonychus and his case that birds descend from theropods.

sections.title: How flight began

sections.title: Birds then and now
sections.summary: Toothed birds of the Cretaceous, the bird lineages that survived, and the American Robin of ORN 101 as a living dinosaur.

chapters.title: The End of the Non-Avian Dinosaurs, and How We Know

sections.title: Paleontology now
sections.summary: CT scans, the Paleobiology Database, new species named every year, and how to follow new discoveries.

preface:
This book is for anyone who has stood under a dinosaur skeleton and wanted to know more than its name. We begin with what a dinosaur actually is, which is more surprising than it sounds, and with how fossils form and how rocks are dated. Then we meet the big groups, look inside their bones to see how fast they grew, follow their footprints, and examine the feathered fossils that changed how we picture them. The book ends with the asteroid that struck 66 million years ago, and with the dinosaurs that survived it.

Those survivors are the birds. If you have read our Birds book (ORN 101), you have already met the American Robin as a living dinosaur; here you will see the evidence from the other side of that story. You will also keep a dinosaur file. In Chapter 1 you choose one dinosaur, and in every chapter after you add what you have learned about it, using the Paleobiology Database, the same open database scientists use.

Paleontology changes every year, as new fossils are found and old ones are studied with new tools. So each chapter separates what is settled from what is still argued, and every claim comes with the evidence behind it. By the end you will know not just what we think about dinosaurs, but how we know it.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a field paleontologist would: from fossils in the ground and in museum drawers, from rock layers and their dates, and from the lab methods (thin sections, CT scans, chemistry) that let bones answer questions.
bible.promise: By the last page you will know what a dinosaur is, how dinosaurs lived and died, why birds count as dinosaurs, and how paleontologists know all of it.
threads: How we know: every claim is tied to fossils, rocks and methods (dating, bone microstructure, trackways, CT scans, chemistry).
Birds are living dinosaurs: evolution connects the Mesozoic to the backyard (ORN 101).
Science changes its mind with evidence: the picture of dinosaurs has been redrawn many times, and some questions are still open.
Deep time is real time: keep the scale of millions of years in view.

runningExamples.name: Tyrannosaurus rex

runningExamples.name: Triceratops
runningExamples.use: The ornithischian representative, and a witness to the final Cretaceous world in the Hell Creek Formation (Chapter 8).

runningExamples.name: Archaeopteryx
runningExamples.use: The fossil link between feathered dinosaurs and birds, shared with ORN 101.

runningExamples.name: The American Robin
runningExamples.use: The living dinosaur from ORN 101, compared with its Mesozoic relatives in Chapters 1, 5 and 7.

runningExamples.name: Your dinosaur file
runningExamples.use: The reader picks one dinosaur in Chapter 1 and adds to its file every chapter, using the Paleobiology Database.

conventions: Genus names capitalized and italic (Tyrannosaurus), species as Tyrannosaurus rex at first mention, T. rex after; English group names lowercase (theropods).
Say 'non-avian dinosaurs' whenever birds are excluded, since birds are dinosaurs.
Ages in millions of years ago with the geologic period; metric units with a familiar comparison; body sizes, masses and speeds as estimated ranges.
Label settled findings and open debates as such.
Cross-reference ORN 101 by chapter (birds as dinosaurs is its Chapter 1).

Open scientific database of fossil occurrences; the reader's research tool for the dinosaur file.

bible.care: Where the science is unsettled (how the main dinosaur branches connect, how aquatic Spinosaurus was, the role of Deccan volcanism, how flight began, how warm-blooded particular dinosaurs were), present the main views with their evidence and say the question is open. Sizes, masses, speeds and colors are estimates; give ranges and say how they were made. If religious objections to deep time or evolution arise, describe the scientific evidence plainly and respectfully, without disparaging anyone's faith. Safety and law: fossil collecting is regulated in many places, and vertebrate fossils on public land usually require a permit; challenges use photographs, museum collections and databases rather than collecting.
